:::{#exm-best-constant-auto}
#### The best constant prediction of fuel economy

Take the 392 cars in the Auto data [described on the limit theorems page](limit-theorems.qmd#exm-clt-auto) as the whole population,
and predict the fuel economy (`mpg`) of a car drawn at random with one number $c$.
The code below computes the expected squared error of three constants,
and sets each beside the right side of @eq-constant-prediction-decompose.

```{r}
#| label: best-constant-auto
#| code-fold: false
auto <- readr::read_csv("data/auto.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
mpg <- auto$mpg
mu <- mean(mpg)
squared_deviations <- (mpg - mu)^2
sigma2 <- mean(squared_deviations)

median_mpg <- median(mpg)
c_values <- c(mean = mu, median = median_mpg, twenty = 20)
constants <- names(c_values)

errors_by_car <- outer(mpg, c_values, "-")
squared_errors <- errors_by_car^2
errors <- colMeans(squared_errors)
shift_squared <- (mu - c_values)^2

tibble::tibble(
  constant = constants,
  c = c_values,
  expected_squared_error = errors,
  decomposition = sigma2 + shift_squared
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# The prose claims 392 cars, that the two columns agree,
# and that the mean is best.
n_cars <- length(mpg)
decomposition <- sigma2 + shift_squared
columns_agree <- all.equal(errors, decomposition)
best_index <- which.min(errors)
mean_error <- errors[["mean"]]
mean_error_matches <- all.equal(mean_error, sigma2)
stopifnot(
  n_cars == 392L,
  !anyNA(mpg),
  columns_agree,
  best_index == 1,
  mean_error_matches
)
```

@fig-best-constant-auto plots the expected squared error of every constant from 10 to 40 against $c$,
and marks the three constants in the table.

```{r}
#| label: fig-best-constant-auto
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Expected squared error of a constant prediction c of fuel economy
#|   for the 392 cars in the Auto data, for c from 10 to 40 miles per gallon.
#|   The points mark the mean, the median and c = 20.
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   A U-shaped curve of expected squared error against the constant c,
#|   lowest at about 23.4 miles per gallon.
#|   Points on the curve mark the mean, which is at the bottom,
#|   the median, which sits just to the left of it,
#|   and c = 20, which sits higher on the left arm.
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6
#| code-fold: true
c_grid <- seq(10, 40, length.out = 301)
grid_deviations <- outer(mpg, c_grid, "-")
grid_squared <- grid_deviations^2
grid_errors <- colMeans(grid_squared)
curve <- tibble::tibble(c = c_grid, expected_squared_error = grid_errors)
point_labels <- c("mean", "median", "c = 20")
label_hjust <- c(0.5, 0.5, 1)
label_vjust <- c(2.5, -2.5, -2)
marked <- tibble::tibble(
  point_label = point_labels,
  c = c_values,
  expected_squared_error = errors,
  label_hjust = label_hjust,
  label_vjust = label_vjust
)
curve_aes <- ggplot2::aes(x = c, y = expected_squared_error)
label_aes <- ggplot2::aes(
  label = point_label,
  hjust = label_hjust,
  vjust = label_vjust
)

ggplot2::ggplot(curve, curve_aes) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = marked, size = 3) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(label_aes, data = marked) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "constant prediction c (miles per gallon)",
    y = "expected squared error"
  ) +
  ggplot2::expand_limits(y = 0) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

The two columns agree, as @thm-constant-prediction-decompose says.
The mean, `{r} round(mu, 2)`, has the smallest expected squared error, `{r} round(sigma2, 2)`,
which is the [variance](#def-variance) of `mpg` over these cars (divisor the number of cars, not one fewer),
as @cor-best-constant says;
the median and $c = 20$ are each worse by $\sqf{\mean - c}$.

:::
